description: Somos estudiantes de primer semestre de Ingeniería de Software en la USCO. Nuestro enfoque actual está centrado en la recolección de información, análisis de necesidades, planeación estructurada de soluciones y su alineación con los ODS.
summary:
El Despertar de la Bitácora (The Awakening of the Logbook) is an English-language browser game that introduces school-age players to the hardware NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars. Players become Squirrel, an astronaut squirrel exploring 3D lunar and Martian landscapes in search of ten lost objects: from the Apollo laser retroreflector, the Lunar Roving Vehicle and Surveyor 3 to Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Viking, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity.

Each object opens a 2D platformer level built around what that mission actually did. Phoenix’s level is solved by scanning for buried ice, and InSight’s by sending seismic pulses through Mars’s crust, mantle and core. Winning a level returns the object to the 3D world with a short animated video, made from real NASA photographs, and a log entry that explains its science, its current status and the NASA source behind each fact. Every recovered object also becomes a power-up for the rest of the game, so players learn by doing, not just by reading.

Because every animation and fact is grounded in real NASA imagery and official data, the game also reaches beyond students to anyone curious about authentic mission photos and verified science. By turning abandoned equipment into memories worth recovering, it shows that this hardware isn’t debris on other worlds, but milestones of exploration whose science still matters.
details:
What it does and how it works

El Despertar de la Bitácora is a browser game that combines two kinds of play. In the 3D world, players control Squirrel, an astronaut squirrel, and walk across the Moon and Mars. Each world has its own physics and atmosphere: lower gravity on the Moon, and wind, dust devils and micrometeorite impacts on Mars. Ten historic NASA objects are hidden across both worlds: the Apollo laser retroreflector, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, Surveyor 3, the Apollo descent stage, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Viking, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity.

Touching an object opens a 2D platformer level designed around what that mission actually did. Players descend a deep canyon by braking their fall (Viking), cross sinking sand by scanning for buried ice (Phoenix), and send seismic pulses through Mars’s crust, mantle and core (InSight). Winning a level brings the object back to the 3D world with a short animated video made from real NASA photographs. A log entry then explains the object’s science, its current status and the source of each fact. Every recovered object becomes a power-up stored in the player’s inventory, so knowledge turns into a new ability.

Benefits and intended impact

The game shows school-age players the history and science behind the hardware left on other worlds by letting them experience it, not just read about it. Each mechanic is tied to a real scientific idea, so learning happens through play. Because the animations use real NASA imagery and every fact comes from official sources (NSSDCA, NASA Science and NASA/JPL), the game also appeals to anyone curious about authentic mission photos and verified data. Our goal is for players to see abandoned equipment not as debris, but as milestones of exploration that are still worth remembering.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript, packaged as a single web page that runs in any modern browser with no installation.
  • Three.js for the 3D worlds, procedural terrain and character models.
  • HTML5 Canvas for the 2D platformer levels.
  • Web Audio API for all synthesized audio: 8-bit chiptune music in the 2D levels, calm ambient soundtracks in the 3D worlds, and sound effects. The game also includes an original song composed by our team.
  • Web Speech API for the narrator’s voice, with subtitles.
  • Tailwind CSS for the interface.
  • Short animations created from real NASA photographs.

Creativity

The game blends two genres: free 3D exploration and classic 2D platforming. Instead of reusing the same challenge, each of the ten levels is built around its object’s real mission, from bouncing lasers off mirrors for the retroreflector to building a launch platform for the descent stage. The story frames the whole adventure as recovering lost memories, which gives every discovery emotional weight.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific accuracy: we only used facts we could verify against NASA sources, and we removed claims we could not confirm.
  • Audience: a gradual difficulty curve, a guide toward the next objective, and short texts suited to school-age players.
  • Accessibility: the game runs on both desktop and mobile, with touch controls, adjustable graphics quality, camera sensitivity, and separate volume settings for music, effects and voice.
  • Engagement: each level asks players to use the power-up from the previous one, which rewards progress and reinforces what they learned.
